metadata.file_name: Comparative indices of the education quality from the opinions of teachers and principals in TALIS 2018.pdf
metadata.title: Comparative indices of the education quality from the opinions of teachers and principals in TALIS 2018

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2018 lower secondary school data collected from teachers and school principals via OECD questionnaires, and then constructs country/economy-level indices (TOI for teachers and POI for principals) from OECD-reported indicator scores. The paper does not report applying TALIS sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures in its own computations; instead, it relies on OECD’s already-produced country indicator tables and uses 95% confidence intervals to classify countries relative to the OECD average. Because the analysis is index construction and cross-country comparisons (including quartile-based ranking and Pearson correlations with PISA 2018 domain scores), the manuscript does not specify any weight variable (e.g., TOTWGT or W_FSTUWT) or any complex-survey variance estimation step. Analysts replicating this work should use the OECD TALIS 2018 technical documentation to determine whether weights are needed for any re-computation at the microdata level; however, for the presented approach based on published country indicator values, weighting is not operationalized in the paper.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper does not model cognitive achievement scores with TALIS plausible values; instead, it constructs indices from OECD TALIS 2018 indicator percentages and confidence-interval classifications based on teachers’ and principals’ questionnaire responses. Because the dependent quantities are derived from published country/economy indicator tables (not from student-level PV-based achievement scales), plausible values are not applicable. The manuscript also does not describe any microdata missingness handling protocol because it does not report an original student/teacher-level analytic dataset or an imputation/deletion strategy.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The paper does not construct a microdata analytic sample from TALIS 2018; instead, it uses OECD TALIS 2018 country/economy indicator tables (teachers’ and principals’ indicator scores) and then applies a rule-based classification using OECD 95% confidence intervals (above/below/not different from the OECD average). It focuses on lower secondary education (TALIS 2018’s target level) and builds indices for each country/economy by theme and by Volume (V1 learning environment; V2 working conditions/well-being), using the set of teacher indicators (T1–T50) and principal indicators (P1–P11) specified in the OECD reports. The only explicit handling of missingness is at the indicator-table level: for example, the French Community of Belgium is noted as having no data in V1 and V1&V2, which affects its placement in the Top/Bottom groups. No additional inclusion/exclusion criteria (e.g., teacher response thresholds, school response thresholds, or complete-case rules) are applied by the authors beyond what is already embedded in the OECD’s published TALIS indicator values.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict well-being, finding that This study is a comparative, index-based analysis using TALIS 2018 lower secondary questionnaires administered to teachers and school principals across 48 countries/economies. The authors construct two rule-based country indices—TOI (teachers’ opinions) and POI (principals’ opinions)—by classifying each OECD TALIS indicator as favourable, unfavourable, or neutral and then aggregating these classifications within themes and across TALIS Volumes V1 (learning environment) and V2 (working conditions/well-being). They report quartile-based Top–Bottom groupings and compute Pearson correlations between the TALIS indices and PISA 2018 domain scores (Reading, Mathematics, Science) at the country/economy level. No machine-learning models are trained; instead, the paper uses descriptive comparisons, confidence-interval-based classifications, and correlation statistics. Limitations include the absence of microdata-level weighting/missing-data procedures in the manuscript and the fact that correlations between country-level indices and PISA outcomes do not establish causal relationships. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This is not an empirical predictive/ML paper: it constructs indices from already-published TALIS 2018 country indicator tables and performs cross-country comparisons and Pearson correlations with PISA 2018. Consequently, fields related to ML algorithms, plausible-value handling for achievement prediction, and missing-data imputation/deletion at the microdata level are not applicable or not reported. The country-level nature of the analysis also means there is no student-level analytic sample size to extract, and no survey-weight variable is operationalized in the authors’ computations.
